The last night of a kingdom

The novel

History has already chosen its ending.

By the time dawn reaches the copper roofs, the victors will have names for everything. Courage will belong to one shore. Wickedness will belong to the other. A complicated war will be cleaned, polished and made simple enough to sing.

But dawn has not yet arrived.

Night lies warm upon the city. Salt gathers on the palace screens. The corridors smell of sesame oil, wet stone and jasmine bruised beneath hurried feet. From the kitchens comes woodsmoke and the sweetness of coconut; from the harbour, tar, fish and rope soaked by the southern sea. Servants carry clean linen past wounded soldiers. Somewhere below, a carpenter is still being asked to mend a hinge—as though the palace expects another season.

In an upper room, a king waits with a man who was not expected to return. Before them are four hours, a jug of water and the small practical decisions by which a kingdom continues while it is ending.

The king has been a scholar, musician, builder, brother, husband and ruler. He has opened granaries during bad rains and closed his hand when mercy would have cost him pride. He is clever enough to recognise his mistakes and human enough to rename them.

Outside, an army prepares the story that generations will inherit. Inside, two men examine the one that will disappear.

No gods. No demons. Only gifted, frightened human beings—and the explanations by which they learn to live with what they have done.
